_comment: SIG-109: few-shot exemplars for the LOGIC specialist ONLY. Wired into the logic role prompt via pr-review-specialists.ts (NOT the shared block). Balanced on purpose. The GOOD examples cover the shapes the logic lens should fire on: AST-rule-backed correctness bugs (the no-dupe-switch-case / no-unsafe-negation / etc. pack), AND — critically — bugs that have NO deterministic backing at all (off-by-one, broken invariant, wrong operator, swapped arguments) but are CONCRETELY ANCHORED to a changed symbol on an added line. Those LLM-only findings are the high-value core of this lens; the SIG-109 validator KEEPS them on the concrete-token anchor, so the exemplars must read as clearly KEEP-worthy. The BAD examples are the FP shapes the validator drops: vague unanchored 'this could be buggy', a logic claim with no concrete code token, taste/style dressed as logic, and a finding anchored to a file the PR did not change. Each example is a (situation, emit_or_not, why) triple — compact, not full JSON, to keep prompt size reasonable.

examples.situation: An added line changes a loop bound to `for (let i = 0; i <= arr.length; i++)` and indexes `arr[i]` inside the body.

finding.headline: `<= arr.length` reads one past the end of `arr`
finding.body: The loop guard uses `<=`, so the final iteration accesses `arr[arr.length]` which is `undefined`. Use `<` to stop at the last valid index.

examples.why: No deterministic scanner emits this — it's an LLM-only correctness call. But it's CONCRETELY ANCHORED: it names `arr.length` and the `<=` token, both on the added line, on a changed path. This is the high-value core of the logic lens and must read as a clear KEEP.

examples.situation: An added line calls `clamp(max, min, value)` but the helper's signature is `clamp(value, min, max)`.

finding.headline: `clamp` arguments are passed in the wrong order
finding.body: `clamp(max, min, value)` swaps the value and bounds — `clamp` expects `(value, min, max)`, so the result is clamped against the wrong range. Reorder to `clamp(value, min, max)`.

examples.why: A real bug with no deterministic backing, anchored to the `clamp` call on a changed line. Names the exact symbol and the argument order. KEEP — this is exactly what the logic lens exists to catch.

examples.situation: A diff changes `getUser` to return `null` when the cache misses, but a caller on a nearby added line does `getUser(id).name` without a null check.

finding.headline: `getUser(id).name` dereferences a now-nullable return
finding.body: This PR makes `getUser` return `null` on a cache miss, but `getUser(id).name` assumes a user object and will throw on the miss path. Guard the result before reading `.name`.

examples.why: Invariant break the diff introduced — no scanner detects it. Anchored to the `getUser(id).name` expression and the `.name` access on a changed line. KEEP.

examples.situation: An added line writes `if (!key in allowed) { reject() }`. The [AST RULE FINDINGS] block carries an `ast/no-unsafe-negation` hit at this path/line.

finding.headline: `!key in allowed` negates `key` before the membership test
finding.body: `!` binds tighter than `in`, so this evaluates `(!key) in allowed` — testing whether the string `"true"`/`"false"` is a key, not whether `key` is absent. Use `!(key in allowed)`.

examples.why: Concrete bug corroborated by a co-located deterministic AST hit (`no-unsafe-negation`). Anchored token (`!key in allowed`) on a changed line. KEEP — and the AST co-location makes it ironclad.

examples.situation: A `switch` gains a second `case "refunded":` clause on an added line; the [AST RULE FINDINGS] block carries an `ast/no-dupe-switch-case` hit there.

finding.headline: Duplicate `case "refunded"` — the second clause is dead
finding.body: Two `case "refunded":` labels exist in this switch; the second can never run because the first matches first. Remove the duplicate or correct the intended status.

examples.why: Deterministic AST hit plus a concrete anchored token (`case "refunded"`). KEEP.

examples.situation: An added line guards a retry with `if (attempts = MAX)` instead of `===`.

finding.headline: `attempts = MAX` assigns instead of comparing
finding.body: The guard uses `=` (assignment) not `===`, so it always sets `attempts` to `MAX` and the branch is always truthy. Use `attempts === MAX`.

examples.why: High-severity correctness bug, anchored to the `attempts = MAX` token on a changed line. No deterministic fact needed — the concrete-token anchor is enough. KEEP.

examples.situation: A new `average` function on added lines does `return sum / items.length` with no guard for an empty `items`.

finding.headline: `average` divides by zero on empty `items`
finding.body: `sum / items.length` returns `NaN` when `items` is empty, which then poisons downstream math. Return `0` (or guard) for the empty case.

examples.why: Edge case the diff didn't handle — no scanner flags it. Anchored to `items.length` and the division on changed lines. KEEP.

examples.situation: Added lines check `if (!cache.has(key))` then later `cache.set(key, await fetch(key))` with an `await` between the check and the set.

finding.headline: TOCTOU between `cache.has(key)` check and `cache.set` after the await
finding.body: The `await fetch(key)` between the `has` check and the `set` lets a concurrent caller populate `key`, so two fetches race and the second overwrites the first. Re-check after the await or store an in-flight promise.

examples.why: Concurrency bug, LLM-only, anchored to `cache.has(key)` / `cache.set` / the `await` on changed lines. KEEP.

examples.situation: Added lines do `try { await reserveStock(sku, qty) } catch (e) {}` and then, AFTER the try, `return { reserved: true }` — an empty catch, and the reservation is reported successful even when `reserveStock` threw.

finding.headline: Empty catch swallows the `reserveStock` failure, then `{ reserved: true }` returns anyway
finding.body: `catch (e) {}` discards a failed `reserveStock`, and the function returns `{ reserved: true }` after the try regardless — callers treat unreserved stock as reserved. Rethrow, or return success only inside the try after a successful reserve.

examples.why: EMIT — both halves of the swallowed-error shape are present and anchored: the catch is EMPTY (suppresses) AND the success commit (`return { reserved: true }`) runs after the try regardless of failure. KEEP. (Contrast the rethrow SKIP below, where the catch propagates.)

examples.situation: An async handler calls `auditLog.record(event)` (an async I/O call) with NO `await` and NO `return`, then immediately `return res.json({ ok: true })`.

finding.headline: `auditLog.record(event)` is not awaited — the write can outlive the response and its rejection is unhandled
finding.body: `auditLog.record(event)` returns a promise that is neither awaited nor returned, yet the handler returns `res.json({ ok: true })` immediately. The write may not finish before the worker is recycled, and a rejection has no handler. Await it (or explicitly `void`-handle with a catch) before returning success.

examples.why: EMIT — a floating promise from an async I/O call followed by an unconditional success return. No scanner detects it; anchored to the `auditLog.record(event)` call on a changed line. This is the high-value logic core. KEEP.

examples.situation: A diff touches a parser; the finding says the change 'could introduce subtle bugs' without naming any symbol, line, or behavior.

finding.headline: This change could introduce subtle bugs
finding.body: The refactor here is risky and might break edge cases; the author should double-check the logic carefully.

examples.why: No concrete code token, no named symbol, no specific behavior — a vague unanchored sev>=4 logic claim. The SIG-109 validator drops this as unanchored-logic-claim. State the exact bug or drop the finding.

examples.situation: The finding describes a real-sounding off-by-one but anchors it to `src/lib/legacy.ts`, a file this PR does NOT change.

finding.headline: Loop in `renderRows` is off-by-one
finding.body: The `renderRows` loop overruns by one element.

examples.why: Pre-existing code the PR didn't touch — no anchor on a changed path. Findings must target lines this PR added or modified. The validator has no changed-path anchor here, so it drops it. Belongs on a separate ticket.

examples.situation: An added line renames a variable to a longer name; the finding objects to the naming choice and calls it a logic problem.

finding.headline: `temporaryResultAccumulator` is too verbose
finding.body: This variable name is unnecessarily long; a shorter name would read better.

examples.why: Taste-level naming disagreement, not a correctness bug. Naming is the author's call (see review discipline). The logic lens fires on broken behavior, not style preferences.

examples.situation: A finding asserts 'the ordering of the two operations is now wrong' but names no function, variable, or line and quotes no code.

finding.headline: The operations now run in the wrong order
finding.body: The two steps appear to be sequenced incorrectly after this change.

examples.why: Plausible-sounding but names no concrete symbol and quotes no code token from the added lines. With nothing to anchor, the validator can't distinguish it from a hallucination — it drops as unanchored-logic-claim. Name the two operations and the correct order, or drop it.

examples.situation: A finding restates what the diff did ('this PR switches the map to a Set') and frames it as a concern without identifying any actual problem.

finding.headline: Switched the collection from a Map to a Set
finding.body: This change replaces the Map with a Set.

examples.why: Describes the change rather than surfacing a problem — the author can see their own diff. Not a finding. (See review discipline: NEVER describe the change that was made.)

examples.situation: An added line uses `==` to compare a number against a string-typed config value; behavior is correct today but the loose equality is fragile.

finding.headline: Loose `==` between `port` (number) and `cfg.port` (string)
finding.body: `port == cfg.port` relies on coercion; if `cfg.port` becomes `"08"` or empty the comparison silently flips. Parse `cfg.port` and use `===`.

examples.why: Concrete, anchored (`port`, `cfg.port`, the `==` token on a changed line) but lower severity (score 3, below the validator's sev>=4 bar so it always keeps). A good, specific finding — included to show the lens can fire below the gate threshold too.

examples.situation: An added line computes `sinceMs = Date.now() - hours * 60 * 60 * 1000`, and you suspect `hours * 60 * 60 * 1000` could overflow or go negative for a large `hours`. But three lines up, `hours` is set via `Math.min(parsed, MAX_RUNS_WINDOW_HOURS)` where `MAX_RUNS_WINDOW_HOURS = 24 * 90` (2160), and `parsed` is already guarded by `Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed > 0`.

cleared.hypothesis: hours * 60 * 60 * 1000 could overflow or produce a negative epoch for large hours
cleared.mitigation: Math.min(parsed, MAX_RUNS_WINDOW_HOURS) clamps hours to 2160 before the multiply (product ~7.8e9, far under Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER); Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed > 0 rules out NaN/Infinity

examples.why: SKIP — refuted by an in-code mitigation. The `Math.min(parsed, 2160)` clamp caps the product far under `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` and the `Number.isFinite` guard rules out NaN/Infinity. A concern your own reasoning concludes is 'theoretical' or 'already clamped' is a CLEAR: record it in `clearedLogicCandidates` quoting the `Math.min(...)` mitigation, do NOT emit a finding. This is the exact self-refuting-finding FP (PR #12 `sinceMs`) that SIG-308 targets.

examples.situation: Added lines wrap a send in `try { await notifyShipped(order) } catch (e) { metrics.inc("notify.fail"); throw e }` — the catch records a metric and RE-THROWS; nothing after the try assumes success.

cleared.hypothesis: the catch swallows a failed notifyShipped so the failure is hidden
cleared.mitigation: the catch re-throws (`throw e`) after the metric, so the failure propagates to the caller — it is not suppressed

examples.why: SKIP — a catch that re-throws is NOT swallowing. This FP fires when a reviewer sees `try/catch` around an I/O call and assumes suppression without reading the `throw e`. Both halves are required for a swallow (suppress + commit-anyway); here neither holds. Record a `clearedLogicCandidate` quoting `throw e`; do not emit.

examples.situation: A retryable queue consumer calls `mailer.send(msg, { dedupKey: msg.id })` — the send passes a dedup key derived from the message id.

cleared.hypothesis: a redelivered message double-sends the email
cleared.mitigation: the send passes `{ dedupKey: msg.id }` — a redelivery with the same id is deduplicated by the mailer, so the effect runs at most once

examples.why: SKIP — a retryable side effect that passes a VISIBLE dedup/idempotency key is idempotent by design. The FP fires when a reviewer sees a send in a consumer and cries double-send without reading the key. Record a `clearedLogicCandidate` quoting `dedupKey`; do not emit. (A send/charge/enqueue with NO such key or dedup lookup in sight IS a real bug — only a present, quotable key clears it.)

examples.situation: A Stripe webhook handler charges `order.amountCents` and passes `{ idempotencyKey: event.id }` to `stripe.charges.create(...)`; the only concern visible in the diff is retry/redelivery of the same webhook event.

cleared.hypothesis: a retried webhook double-charges the order
cleared.mitigation: the Stripe call passes `{ idempotencyKey: event.id }`, so redelivery of the same event reuses the same idempotency key

examples.why: SKIP — for the retry/redelivery hypothesis, a visible delivery-stable idempotency key is enough; do not require an additional `order.paid` / status guard for the SAME retry. Keep the recall valve: if the diff visibly shows `event.id` is fresh per attempt or that different event ids can represent the same logical operation, then the key is not stable and the missing domain-state guard remains a real bug.

examples.situation: Added middleware: `if (!allowed) { return res.status(429).end() }` and on the NEXT line `handler(req, res)`. A reviewer flags `handler` runs unconditionally after the 429 (double response / guard bypass).

cleared.hypothesis: handler runs unconditionally after the 429 is sent, causing a double response / bypassing the guard
cleared.mitigation: the guard branch ends in `return res.status(429).end()` — the early return means the tail line only runs on the allowed path; it is the else-path, not unconditional

examples.why: SKIP — before flagging that a tail call (`next()`, a commit, a success return, a handler) 'runs unconditionally' or 'after the error response', look for an early `return`/`throw` inside the error branch. In JavaScript/TypeScript, a `return` inside an `if` exits the enclosing function/callback, not just the block, so the code after the `if` is the else-path. This is a control-flow misread — quote the `return` in a `clearedLogicCandidate`, do not emit. (Only a branch that sends the error and then FALLS THROUGH with no return/throw is the real double-response bug.)

examples.situation: Added `const name = String(input.name ?? "anonymous")` then `greet(name)`. A reviewer flags `String(undefined)` yields the literal "undefined" / a NaN / an empty-value bug.

cleared.hypothesis: String(input.name) is "undefined" when input.name is missing, corrupting downstream use
cleared.mitigation: `?? "anonymous"` (a nullish-coalescing default) handles the null/undefined branch BEFORE String() runs, so String(undefined) never occurs

examples.why: SKIP — a nullish-coalescing default (`?? d`) or an explicit null/undefined check applied to a value before it is used covers the null/undefined branch, so do not claim a downstream `String(undefined)` / NaN bug past it; quote the `?? d` in a `clearedLogicCandidate`. CRITICAL DISTINCTION — this clears `??` ONLY, NOT `||`: `x || d` clobbers EVERY falsy value (0, '', false, NaN), so `count || 10` / `config.retries || 3` silently replaces a VALID 0/''/false with the default — that is the real falsy-zero BUG and you MUST still flag it whenever x can legitimately be 0/''/false. (A raw use with NO null-guard at all is also in scope.)

examples.situation: A diff adds a `maxLength` check to the `title` field of a form validator. A reviewer flags that the validator 'does not also check the unrelated, untouched `description` and `tags` fields.'

cleared.hypothesis: the validator fails to check the description and tags fields
cleared.mitigation: the diff added a check to the one field it touched; description/tags are pre-existing untouched fields, not a defect this change introduced

examples.why: SKIP — demanding handling for inputs or branches the diff did NOT add or change is a scope-expansion wishlist, not a defect in the changed code; assume untouched behavior is intentional. IMPORTANT — this is ONLY about UNTOUCHED paths: a guard or precondition that is MISSING on the path the diff DID add/change IS in scope and you MUST flag it. A newly-added branch that performs a state change / write / refund WITHOUT a required precondition the operation needs (e.g. a new refund path that never checks the order was paid) is a real introduced bug — flag it; do not mistake it for scope-creep.
